newsitem.title: USA: U.S. $1 coin could save millions but hurt tourism.
newsitem.headline: U.S. $1 coin could save millions but hurt tourism.

text.p: The future of a popular tourist spot -- the Bureau of Engraving and Printing plant near the Mall -- as well as vast potential cost savings are at stake in the fight over a new U.S. $1 coin.

"Eliminating the one-dollar note could substantially reduce, and possibly eliminate, the need for a Washington, D.C., production plant," the General Accounting Office said Thursday in a look at coinage and money-printing operations.

Bill printing could be consolidated in Fort Worth, Texas, if a $1 coin were issued in place of the note, GAO officials said. They said the bureau preferred to have a back-up plant but had not decided whether to replace the Washington plant.
The Bureau of Engraving and Printing says 700,000 people a year visit the plant, which prints bills in denominations from $1 to $100.

Members of a House Banking subcommittee were sceptical a $1 coin would be a success, given the lackluster record of the Susan B. Anthony dollar coin. Nor were some of them ready to stop producing the $1 bill, a key premise in GAO's estimate that the $1 coin would save $456 million a year in costs.
Coins can last 30 years but paper notes must be replaced every 16 months at government expense.
"These are not false savings," said Michael Motley, GAO associate director for government business operations, who said other nations successfully converted to coins.
"Well, fine, you run on that platform," retorted Representative Joe Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat.

Public acceptance of a $1 coin could rise, Motley said, if it had a distinctive colour or if a new design was adopted. The Anthony coin honouring the women's sufferage leader was faulted as too similar in size and appearance to the 25-cent coin.

The U.S. Mint no longer produces the Anthony dollar but has a three-year supply stockpiled. It estimates it would take 30 months to develop and begin production of a new $1 coin if Congress ordered it.
GAO said the mint could resume production of the Anthony dollar if supplies ran out and a new $1 coin was not ordered.

But Representative Floyd Flake, New York Democrat, said paper notes were lighter and easier to carry than $1 coins. He was not mollified by a suggestion that more $2 bills could be printed if a $1 coin was mandated. "It's a pain in the butt to carry all those coins in your pocket," Flake said.

In the past five years the $1 bill accounted for 47 percent of notes produced by the Bureau of Engraving and Printing. It could cost $73 million to gear up to produce a $1 coin, according to the mint. A new bill-printing plant could cost from $158 million to $250 million.
